summary: Extends the BGP Tunnel Encapsulation attribute to support IPsec tunnels, in addition to other encapsulations such as GRE and L2TPv3. It was replaced by RFC 9012.

eli5.summary: Routers can announce which kinds of tunnels they accept. This note adds secure IPsec tunnels to the list. It was later replaced by RFC 9012.

subtitle: Adding secure tunnels to BGP's tunnel type announcements

tldr.problem: Border Gateway Protocol allows routers to announce which types of tunnels they support for different routes. The initial version supported GRE, L2TPv3 and IP-in-IP tunnels, but not IPsec.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5566 extends the BGP Tunnel Encapsulation attribute with new tunnel types for IPsec in tunnel mode, plus variants where IPsec protects other tunnels in transport mode.
tldr.outcome: Routers can now signal IPsec tunnel support via BGP, enabling automated secure tunnel setup. This RFC was replaced by RFC 9012 in 2021.

today: RFC 9012 replaced RFC 5566 in 2021. It is the current standard for BGP tunnel encapsulation attributes.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The BGP Tunnel Encapsulation Subsequent Address Family Identifier (SAFI) allows routers to communicate which tunnel types they support and to associate this information with specific routes. RFC 5512 defined the original mechanism and included support for Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE), Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol (L2TPv3), and IP-in-IP tunnels.

RFC 5566 extends this framework to include IPsec as a tunnel type, supporting both IP Authentication Header (AH) and IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) in tunnel mode. It also allows routers to advertise IP-in-IP and MPLS-in-IP tunnels that are protected by IPsec running in transport mode, providing cryptographic security for the outer tunnel headers.
sections.eli5: BGP lets routers tell each other what kinds of tunnels they can use. This adds IPsec tunnels (the secure kind) to what routers can announce.

sections.title: IPsec Tunnel Types
sections.content:
The RFC defines four new tunnel type values in the BGP Tunnel Encapsulation attribute. Transmit tunnel endpoint (type 3) marks a router that will only send traffic through an IPsec tunnel but does not expect to receive tunneled traffic. IPsec in Tunnel-mode (type 4) means the entire IP packet is encrypted and a new IPsec header is added.

IP-in-IP Tunnel with IPsec Transport Mode (type 5) and MPLS-in-IP Tunnel with IPsec Transport Mode (type 6) describe scenarios where IPsec protects the outer tunnel, rather than the inner payload. The distinction matters: tunnel mode encrypts everything end-to-end, while transport mode protects only the tunnel headers, leaving the inner protocol visible to the tunnel endpoints.
sections.eli5: There are different ways to use IPsec with tunnels. It can wrap the whole thing in encryption, or just protect the outer tunnel header. Each way gets a different type number so routers know what to expect.

sections.title: How Routers Use IPsec Tunnel Announcements
sections.content:
When a BGP router receives an Encapsulation SAFI update advertising an IPsec tunnel type from another router (the next hop), it MUST initiate an IPsec Security Association (SA) of the specified type for any data packets destined for that next hop. All such packets MUST be sent through that SA.

Routers that share a network interface are expected to use the same security policy. If one router on an interface requires IPsec for a particular next hop, the receiving router SHOULD also require IPsec for all traffic from other senders on that interface. This prevents complex selector logic trying to distinguish which traffic needs protection, and simplifies administration by treating the interface consistently.
sections.eli5: When a router says it wants IPsec tunnels, the other router sets up the secure connection and uses it for all traffic to that destination.

sections.title: Tunnel Authenticator
sections.content:
RFC 5566 defines an optional IPsec Tunnel Authenticator sub-TLV (sub-TLV type 3) that allows routers to prove their identity during IPsec SA setup. The authenticator contains a type field and a value; the RFC defines authenticator type 1 as a 20-octet SHA-1 hash of the router's public key, as used in IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange version 2).

A router sending the Authenticator sub-TLV must be configured with a private/public key pair. When the receiving router establishes an IPsec SA, it uses IKEv2 to obtain a certificate from the peer and verifies the public key hashes to the value in the sub-TLV. Both routers validate each other's keys before completing SA establishment. To protect the BGP session itself, the RFC strongly recommends using TCP MD5 authentication.
sections.eli5: The authenticator is like a name tag showing which router is which. It uses cryptographic hashes so you can prove you are who you claim to be without sending the actual secret.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
IPsec itself provides authentication and encryption for tunneled traffic, bringing security considerations from RFC 4301 (IPsec Architecture), RFC 4302 (AH), and RFC 4303 (ESP) into play. Any modification of encapsulation information or tunnel type choice can cause packets to be misrouted or dropped, though IPsec protection makes misdelivery less harmful because authentication or decryption will fail at the receiver.

If the BGP session itself is not protected, an attacker could mount a denial-of-service attack by establishing many bogus BGP sessions and forcing SA creation for each. However, the RFC notes that such an attacker could damage the entire routing system anyway. The session protection recommendation above (TCP MD5) mitigates this risk. RFC 5566 was obsoleted by RFC 9012 in 2021, which is the current standard for BGP tunnel encapsulation attributes.
sections.eli5: IPsec is already secure, but someone could trick routers by sending fake announcements if the BGP messages are not protected. A newer RFC, 9012, replaced this one.
